'''''Chrozophora tinctoria''''' (commonly known as '''dyer's croton''',<ref name=arsgrin>{{GRIN | accessdate=3 December 2012}}</ref> '''giradol''',<ref name=arsgrin/> '''[[turnsole]]'''<ref name=arsgrin/> or '''dyer's litmus plant'''<ref>{{cite book |last=Shmida |first=Avi |title=MAPA's Dictionary of Plants and Flowers in Israel |publisher=MAPA Publishers |location=Tel-Aviv|year=2005 |page=250|language=he|oclc=716569354}}, s.v. Chrozophora tinctoria</ref>) is a plant species native to the [[Mediterranean]], the [[Middle East]], [[India]], [[Pakistan]], and [[Central Asia]].<ref name="POWO" /><ref>Zervous, S., Raus, T. & Yannitsaros, A. (2009). Additions to the flora of the island of Kalimnos (SE Aegean, Greece). Willdenowia 39: 165-177.</ref><ref>Dobignard, A. & Chatelain, C. (2011). Index synonymique de la flore d'Afrique du nord 3: 1-449. Éditions des conservatoire et jardin botaniques, Genève.</ref> It is also present as a weed in North America and Australia.<ref name="Mifsud">{{cite web |last1=Mifsud |first1=Stephen |title=Chrozophora tinctoria (Dyer's Litmus) |url=http://www.maltawildplants.com/EUPH/Chrozophora_tinctoria.php |website=Wild Plants of Malta |access-date=22 April 2020}}</ref>

==Description==
It is an annual, typically found in nutrient-poor ground.  It develops a large [[taproot]].<ref name="Mifsud"/> The plant is erect and covered with wool-like hairs.<ref name=":0" /> The ash-green leaves are alternate. The tiny [[monecious]] flowers are grouped in a [[raceme]]. The lower, female flowers lack petals and the upper male flowers have five small yellow petals. Pollination is by ants.<ref name="Mifsud"/> The fruits are conspicuous and consist of three dark green conjoined spheres. Their surface is decorated with white scales and warty structures. Each sphere contains three seeds, which are propelled away from the plant by the mechanical force of the mature fruit twisting as it opens.<ref name="Mifsud"/> It is considered a poisonous plant. Its consumption may cause stomach upset, vomiting, nausea, and diarrhoea.<ref name="FH">{{Cite journal | last= Abid, Mushtaq Ahmad, Muhammad Zafar, Sadia Zafar, Mohamed Fawzy Ramadan, Ashwaq T. Althobaiti, Shazia Sultana, Omer Kilic, Trobjon Makhkamov, Akramjon Yuldashev, Oybek Mamarakhimov, Khislat Khaydarov, Afat O. Mammadova, Komiljon Komilov and Salman Majeed|first=Aqsa |date=December 2023|title= Foliar epidermal and trichome micromorphological diversity among poisonous plants and their taxonomic significance|journal=[[Folia Horticulturae]]|language=en|volume=35|issue=2|pages=243–274|doi= 10.2478/fhort-2023-0019 |issn=2083-5965|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
''Chrozophora tinctoria'' was named ''Croton tinctorius'' by [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 1753. The botanist [[Conrad Moench]] classified it in the genus ''[[Ricinoides]]'' in 1794, but the accepted name of the species was created in 1824 when [[Adrien-Henri de Jussieu]] moved it to ''[[Chrozophora]]''. Together with its genus it is part of the [[Euphorbiaceae]] family. It has no accepted [[subspecies]] or [[Variety (botany)|varieties]], but has several among its 30 [[Synonym (botany)|synonyms]].<ref name="POWO">{{Cite POWO |last1=POWO |date=2026 |id=340969-1 |title=''Chrozophora tinctoria'' (L.) A.Juss. |access-date=14 February 2026}}</ref>

==Use for dye==
''Chrozophora  tinctoria'' produced the blue-purple colorant "[[turnsole]]" (also known as katasol<ref name="HeritageSci2018" /> or folium<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last1=Nabais|first1=P.|last2=Oliveira|first2=J.|last3=Pina|first3=F.|last4=Teixeira|first4=N.|last5=de Freitas|first5=V.|last6=Brás|first6=N. F.|last7=Clemente|first7=A.|last8=Rangel|first8=M.|last9=Silva|first9=A. M. S.|last10=Melo|first10=M. J.|date=April 2020|title=A 1000-year-old mystery solved: Unlocking the molecular structure for the medieval blue from Chrozophora tinctoria, also known as folium|journal=Science Advances|language=en|volume=6|issue=16|article-number=eaaz7772|doi=10.1126/sciadv.aaz7772|pmid=32426456|pmc=7164948|bibcode=2020SciA....6.7772N|issn=2375-2548|doi-access=free}}</ref> ) used in medieval [[illuminated manuscript]]s and as a food colorant in Dutch cheese and certain liquors.<ref>[http://www.kremer-pigmente.com/media/pdf/36018e.pdf Chrozophora, Folium cloth]</ref> Its use was mostly as substitute of the more expensive Tyrian purple, the famous dye obtained from Murex molluscs.<ref>M. Aceto, E. Calà, A. Agostino, G. Fenoglio, A. Idone, C. Porte, M. Gulmini, On the identification of folium and orchil on illuminated manuscripts, Spectrochimica Acta Part A: Molecular and Biomolecular Spectroscopy, http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.saa.2016.08.046</ref> The color comes from the plant's fruit, specifically its dry outer coat.<ref name="HeritageSci2018">{{cite journal |last1=Melo |first1=Maria J. |last2=Castro |first2=Rita |last3=Nabais |first3=Paula |last4=Vitorino |first4=Tatiana |title=The book on how to make all the colour paints for illuminating books: unravelling a Portuguese Hebrew illuminators' manual |journal=Heritage Science |date=2018 |volume=6 |page=44 |doi=10.1186/s40494-018-0208-z |doi-access=free }}</ref> The colorant is also obtained from the translucent sap contained in the plant cells when the leaves of the plant are broken off and exposed to the air.<ref name= "Krispil1985">{{cite book|last=Ḳrispil|first=Nissim|title=A Bag of Plants (The Useful Plants of Israel) |publisher=Cana Publishing House Ltd.|volume=3 (Ṭ.-M.) |year=1985|location=Jerusalem|pages=627–629, 632–633 |language=he|isbn=965-264-011-5 |oclc=959573975 }}, s.v. ''Chrozophora tinctoria''</ref> Different shades of blue and purple may also be obtained when the juice extracts are exposed to the vapors emitted from [[ammonia]] (NH<sub>3</sub>), and which in France, during the late 19th century, was produced by applying fresh horse manure and urine to the fabric that was soaked with the plant extract.<ref name= "Krispil1985"/> The plant has historically been used throughout the [[Levant]] to dye clothing.<ref name= "Krispil1985"/> {{convert|100|kg|lb}} of the plant produces {{convert|50|kg|lb}} of sap, and with this quantity one is able to dye {{convert|25|kg|lb}} of fabric rolls.<ref name= "Krispil1985"/>

In 2020, an interdisciplinary team of researchers from [[Faculdade de Ciências e Tecnologia da Universidade Nova de Lisboa|FCT NOVA]], [[University of Porto]] and [[University of Aveiro]], identified the complex chemical structure of the medieval purple-blue dye extracted from the fruits of ''Chrozophora tinctoria''.<ref name=":0" /> The chemical structure of the medieval dye was a mystery until now.<ref name=":0" /> The extracts obtained showed a novel blue chemical, [[chrozophoridine]] as the main chromophore.<ref name=":0" /><ref name="UNDL news">{{cite web |title=1000-Year-Old Mistery Unfolded With The Discovery Of Medieval Blue Dye Structure |date=20 April 2020 |url=https://www.unl.pt/en/news/general/1000-year-old-mistery-unfolded-discovery-medieval-blue-dye-structure |publisher=[[Universidade Nova de Lisboa]] |access-date=22 April 2020}}</ref>
